title: Increased Sodium Chloride Concentration Enhances Piscirickettsia salmonis Epithelial Translocation by Modulating Immune and Osmoregulatory Gene Expression in RTgutGC Cells
content:
ABSTRACT

Climate change is expected to increase seawater salinity, potentially altering the physiological responses of marine organisms. In salmonids, elevated salinity has been associated with outbreaks of infectious diseases; however, the mechanisms linking salinity with intestinal epithelial dysfunction and bacterial invasion remain poorly understood. This study evaluated the effects of increased sodium chloride concentrations on the integrity of the rainbow trout intestinal epithelial cell line RTgutGC and its relationship with P. salmonis translocation. Cells cultured under control (8 g/L NaCl) or hyperosmotic conditions (16 and 20 g/L NaCl) were assessed for cytotoxicity, epithelial integrity, permeability, bacterial translocation, and gene expression. Hyperosmotic conditions significantly increased epithelial permeability and reduced barrier integrity, as evidenced by altered paracellular permeability to Dextran FITC and modulation of tight junction-related genes, including cld-3 and zo-1. Salinity also induced the expression of osmoregulatory (tsc22 and nka) and immune-related genes (il-1β and il-10), indicating activation of response to osmotic stress. Importantly, elevated salinity significantly enhanced the translocation of P. salmonis across the epithelial monolayer, whereas no bacterial translocation was detected under control conditions. Moreover, high salinity increased infection-associated cytotoxicity, mainly at 20 g/L NaCl. Together, these findings demonstrate that increased sodium chloride concentration compromises intestinal epithelial barrier function while promoting P. salmonis translocation. These results provide mechanistic evidence linking climate-driven changes in seawater salinity with increased epithelial susceptibility to bacterial pathogens and suggest that osmotic stress may represent an important environmental factor influencing the pathogenesis of piscirickettsiosis in salmonids.
